title: Book Inventory REST API
summary: A small Go REST API over a single resource: five endpoints, Gin for routing, GORM over Postgres, and configuration read from the environment. Deliberately minimal — the smallest thing that is still a real service.

chapters.title: The surface
paragraphs: Five endpoints over one resource, all under `/api/v1/books`. `GET /books` lists, `GET /books/{id}` fetches one, `POST /books` creates, `PUT /books/{id}` updates, `DELETE /books/{id}` removes. A book is five fields — id, title, author, publisher, quantity. That is the whole API.

Gin handles routing, GORM handles Postgres, and the credentials come out of the environment through dotenv rather than out of the source. There is no pagination on the list endpoint: it returns every row. At this size that is fine, and it is the first thing that would have to change if it were not.
chapters.tradeoff: An unpaginated list endpoint is a latent problem, not a current one. It is correct until the table is large enough to matter, and there is nothing in the code that will tell me when that happens.

chapters.title: Four packages, not four layers
paragraphs: The code is split across four packages — `routes`, `controllers`, `models`, `database`. That is a real separation and it is worth having, but it is not a layered architecture and I want to be precise about the difference, because the two get conflated constantly.

In a layered design the service layer would declare the interface it needs and the storage layer would implement it, so the dependency points inward and either side can be replaced. That is not what this is. The controllers import `database` directly and call `database.DB` on it. There is no interface between them, no service layer, and no way to swap the store without editing every handler.

For five endpoints over one table, that is the right call. An interface with exactly one implementation is indirection with no payoff — it costs a file, a mock and a layer of naming, and buys the ability to do something I have no plan to do. The structure earns its place when there is a second implementation or a second consumer, and here there is neither.
chapters.tradeoff: This is the choice that stops scaling first. The moment there is business logic worth testing without a database, the handlers are the wrong place for it and every one of them has to be opened. I would rather pay that later than pay for a layer I am not using now — but it is deferred cost, not avoided cost.

chapters.title: AutoMigrate, and when it stops being fine
paragraphs: The schema is not in migration files. `database.Connect` calls `db.AutoMigrate(&models.Book{})` on startup, and GORM reconciles the table against the struct — adding columns and indexes to match whatever the Go type currently says.

For a single-developer project with one table this is genuinely good. The struct is the schema, there is no second place to update, and the two cannot drift apart because one of them is derived from the other.

It is also the thing I would replace first on anything with a second developer or a production database. AutoMigrate adds; it does not drop columns, it does not rename, and it does not roll back. It runs on every boot, which means the schema changes at deploy time rather than at a moment anyone chose. And because there are no migration files, there is no record of what the schema looked like last month — the history exists only in the git history of the struct.
chapters.tradeoff: A schema with no migration history is a schema you cannot reason about backwards. I traded reviewability for the fact that there is nothing to keep in sync, which is the right trade at one table and the wrong one at ten.
